en: Majjhima Nikāya 15:
Anumānasutta Thus have I heard—
On one occasion the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna was dwelling among the Bhaggas at Susumāragira, in the Bhesakaḷā Grove, the Deer Park.
There the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna addressed the bhikkhus:
“Friends, bhikkhus!”
“Friend,” those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna.
The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said this:
“If, friend, a bhikkhu invites [you] to choose:”

‘Let the venerable ones speak to me; I am to be spoken to by the venerable ones’—yet he is difficult to speak with, possessed of qualities that make him difficult to speak with, intolerant, and unwilling to accept instruction respectfully.
Then his fellow celibates do not think him one who should be spoken to, nor do they think him one who should be instructed, nor do they place trust in that person.
They think [these things] must be undertaken.
And what, friends, are the qualities that make for being difficult to correct?
Here, friends, a bhikkhu has evil desires and is under the sway of evil desires.
Furthermore, friends, when a bhikkhu has evil desires and is under the sway of evil desires—
this too is a quality that makes one difficult to correct.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu is one who lauds himself and disparages others.
Furthermore, friends, when a bhikkhu is one who praises himself and disparages others—
this too is a quality that makes for difficult speech.
Again, friends, a bhikkhu is prone to anger and is overcome by anger.
Furthermore, friends, when a bhikkhu is prone to anger and is overcome by anger—
this too is a quality that makes one difficult to speak to.
Moreover, friends, a bhikkhu is prone to anger and, on account of that anger, remains resentful.
Furthermore, friends, when a bhikkhu is prone to anger and, on account of anger, is resentful—
this too is a quality that makes one difficult to speak to.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu is prone to anger and, on account of anger, is full of attachment.
Furthermore, friends, when a bhikkhu is prone to anger and is resentful because of that anger—
this too is a quality that makes one difficult to speak to.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu is prone to anger and utters speech bordering on anger.
Furthermore, friends, when a bhikkhu is angry or utters speech out of anger—
this too is a quality that makes one difficult to speak to.
Moreover, friends, when a bhikkhu, being reproved by a reprover, resists the reprover.
Furthermore, friends, when a bhikkhu, being reproved by a reprover, retorts against that reprover—
this too is a quality that makes one difficult to admonish.
Furthermore, friends, when a bhikkhu, being reproved by a reprover, disparages that reprover.
Furthermore, friends, when a bhikkhu, being reproved by a reprover, reviles that reprover—
this too is a quality that makes one difficult to correct.
Furthermore, friends, when a bhikkhu, being reproved by a reprover, counter-accuses that reprover.
Furthermore, friends, when a bhikkhu, being reproved by a reprover, counter-charges the reprover—
this too is a quality that makes for difficult speech.
Furthermore, friends, when a bhikkhu, being reproved by a reprover, evades one matter with another, diverts the talk to an external subject, and displays anger, hatred, and resentment.
Furthermore, friends, when a bhikkhu, being reproved by a reprover, evades one matter with another, diverts the conversation to an external subject, and displays anger, hatred, and resentment—
this too is a quality that makes one difficult to correct.
Furthermore, friends, when a bhikkhu, being reproved by a reprover, does not comply with the charge.
Furthermore, friends, when a bhikkhu, being reproved by a reprover, does not comply with the charge—
this too is a quality that makes one difficult to admonish.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu is one who slanders and is prone to resentment.
Furthermore, friends, when a bhikkhu is contemptuous and insolent—
this too is a quality that makes one difficult to correct.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu is envious and miserly.
Furthermore, friends, when a bhikkhu is envious and avaricious—
this too is a quality that makes one difficult to correct.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu is fraudulent and deceitful.
Furthermore, friends, when a bhikkhu is deceitful and fraudulent—
this too is a quality that makes one difficult to correct.
Moreover, friends, a bhikkhu is stubborn and conceited.
Furthermore, friends, when a bhikkhu is stubborn and conceited—
this too is a quality that makes one difficult to correct.
Moreover, friends, a bhikkhu is one who clings to his own views, holds them tenaciously, and is reluctant to relinquish them.
Furthermore, friends, when a bhikkhu is one who clings to his own views, holds them firmly, and is difficult to disabuse of them—
this too is a quality that makes for being difficult to correct.
These, friends, are called the qualities that make for being difficult to correct.
Friends, when a bhikkhu does not invite correction by saying,
“Let the venerable ones speak to me; I am to be corrected by the venerable ones,” yet he is easy to speak to, possesses the qualities that make one easy to speak to,
is patient, receptive to instruction, and compliant— then his fellow celibates [should address him].
They think he is one who should be spoken to, they think he is one who should be instructed, and they think that confidence should be placed in that person.
And what, friends, are the qualities that make one easy to speak to?
Here, friends, a bhikkhu does not have evil desires, nor is he under the sway of evil desires.
Furthermore, friends, when a bhikkhu does not have evil desires and has not fallen under the sway of evil desires—
this too is a quality that makes one easy to speak to.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu does not praise himself nor disparage others.
Furthermore, friends, when a bhikkhu does not praise himself and does not disparage others—
this too is a quality that makes one easy to speak to.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu is not angry and is not overcome by anger.
Furthermore, friends, that a bhikkhu is not angry and is not overcome by anger—
this too is a quality that makes one easy to speak to.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu is not angry and does not, on account of anger, harbor resentment.
Furthermore, friends, that a bhikkhu is not angry and does not bear a grudge because of anger—
this too is a quality that makes one easy to speak to.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu is not angry and does not become attached because of anger.
Furthermore, friends, when a bhikkhu is not prone to anger and does not become attached for the sake of anger—
this too is a quality that makes one easy to speak to.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu is not prone to anger and does not utter speech bordering on anger.
Furthermore, friends, when a bhikkhu is not prone to anger and does not utter speech bordering on anger—
this too is a quality that makes one easy to speak to.
Furthermore, friends, when a bhikkhu, being reproved by a reprover, does not retort against the reprover.
Furthermore, friends, when a bhikkhu, being reproved by a reprover, does not retort against the reprover—
this too is a quality that makes one easy to speak to.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu, being reproved by a reprover, does not disparage the reprover.
Furthermore, friends, when a bhikkhu, being reproved by a reprover, does not revile the reprover—
this too is a quality that makes one easy to speak to.
Furthermore, friends, when a bhikkhu, being reproved by a reprover, does not counter-charge the reprover.
Furthermore, friends, when a bhikkhu, being reproved by a reprover, does not counter-reprove the reprover— this too is a quality that makes one easy to speak to.

Moreover, friends, when a bhikkhu, being reproved by a reprover, does not evade with one thing after another, does not deflect the conversation to external matters, and does not manifest anger, hatred, or resentment.

Furthermore, friends, when a bhikkhu, being reproved by a reprover, does not evade one matter with another, does not divert the conversation to external topics, and does not manifest anger, hatred, or resentment—
this too is a quality that makes one easy to speak to.
Furthermore, friends, when a bhikkhu, being reproved by a reprover, responds to the reproof.
Furthermore, friends, when a bhikkhu, being reproved by a reprover, makes amends in the matter of his confession—
this too is a quality that makes one easy to speak to.
Moreover, friends, a bhikkhu is not one who slanders and is not one who reviles.
Furthermore, friends, when a bhikkhu is not slanderous and not spiteful—
this too is a quality that makes one easy to speak to.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu is not envious and not miserly.
Furthermore, friends, when a bhikkhu is not envious and is not miserly—
this too is a quality that makes one easy to speak to.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu is not fraudulent and is not deceitful.
Furthermore, friends, when a bhikkhu is not crafty and not deceitful—
this too is a quality that makes him easy to speak to.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu is not stubborn and is not conceited.
Furthermore, friends, when a bhikkhu is not stubborn and is not conceited—
this too is a quality that makes one easy to speak to.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu does not cling to his own views, does not grasp at them tenaciously, and is easy to relinquish [them].
Furthermore, friends, when a bhikkhu does not cling to his own views, does not grasp at them tenaciously, and is easy to let go of them—
this too is a quality that makes one easy to speak to.
These, friends, are called the qualities that make one easy to speak to.
In this regard, friends, a bhikkhu should infer about himself in this way:
"This person who has evil desires and is under the sway of evil desires is displeasing and disagreeable to me;
if I were to have evil desires and be under the sway of evil desires, I too would be displeasing and disagreeable to others."
"Knowing this, friends, a bhikkhu should arouse the thought: 'I shall not have evil desires, nor shall I fall under the power of evil desires.
[He should reflect: 'This person who exalts himself and disparages others is displeasing and disagreeable to me;
if I were to exalt myself and disparage others, I too would be displeasing and disagreeable to others.'"
Knowing this, friends, a bhikkhu should arouse the thought: "I shall not praise myself nor disparage others. He should think:
"This person who is angry and overcome by anger is displeasing and disagreeable to me.
If I were also angry and overcome by anger, I too would be displeasing and disagreeable to others."
Knowing this, friends, a bhikkhu should arouse the thought: "I shall not be angry, nor shall I be overcome by anger. He should reflect:
"This person who is angry and harbors resentment because of anger is displeasing and disagreeable to me;
but if I were also to be angry and harbor resentment because of anger, I too would be displeasing and disagreeable to others."
Knowing this, friends, a bhikkhu should arouse the thought: "I shall not be angry, nor shall I be resentful because of anger.
He should reflect: "This person who is angry and becomes embroiled because of anger is displeasing and disagreeable to me;
if I were to be angry and become embroiled because of anger, I too would be displeasing and disagreeable to others."
Knowing this, friends, a bhikkhu should arouse the thought: "I shall not be angry, nor shall I be one who, because of anger, speaks with attachment.
He should reflect: "This person who is angry and utters speech bordering on anger is displeasing and disagreeable to me;
if I were to be angry and utter speech bordering on anger, I too would be displeasing and disagreeable to others."
Knowing this, friends, a bhikkhu should arouse the thought: "I will not be angry, nor will I utter speech bordering on anger.
He should reflect: "This person who, when reproved by a reprover, retorts to the reprover, is displeasing and disagreeable to me;
if I, being reproved by a reprover, were to retort to the reprover, I too would be displeasing and disagreeable to others."
"Knowing this, friends, a bhikkhu should arouse the thought: 'When reproved by a reprover, I shall not retort against the reprover. He should think:
'This person who, when reproved by a reprover, disparages the reprover—is a person I dislike and do not like.
If I, being reproved by a reprover, were to disparage the reprover, I too would be disliked and disliked by others.'"
Knowing this, friends, a bhikkhu should arouse the thought: "When I am reproved by a reprover, I shall not reject the reprover. He should think:
"This person who, when reproved by a reprover, throws the blame back upon the reprover, is displeasing and disagreeable to me;
if I, being reproved by a reprover, were to throw the blame back upon the reprover, I too would be displeasing and disagreeable to others."
"Knowing this, friends, a bhikkhu should resolve: 'When reproved by a reprover, I will not counter-reprove the reprover.

For that person who, when reproved by a reprover, evades one thing with another, diverts the conversation to external matters, and displays anger, hatred, and resentment—that person is displeasing and disagreeable to me."

‘If, when I am reproved by a reprover, I were to evade one thing with another, were to divert the conversation to an external matter, or were to manifest anger, hatred, and resentment, I too would become unpleasant and disagreeable to others.

Knowing this, friends, a bhikkhu should arouse the thought: ‘When I am reproved by a reprover, I will not evade one thing with another; I will not divert the conversation to an external matter; I will not manifest anger, hatred, and resentment.’”
‘This person who, when reproved by a reprover, does not make amends for the accusation—this person is displeasing and disagreeable to me.
If I, being reproved by a reprover, were likewise not to make amends for the accusation, I too would be displeasing and disagreeable to others.
Knowing this, friends, a bhikkhu should arouse the thought: “When reproved by a reprover, I shall make amends for the accusation.”
‘This person who is contemptuous and insolent is displeasing and disagreeable to me;
if I were also contemptuous and insolent, I too would be displeasing and disagreeable to others.
Knowing this, friends, a bhikkhu should arouse the thought: “I shall be free from contempt and free from insolence.”
‘This person who is envious and miserly is displeasing and disagreeable to me;
if I were envious and miserly, I too would be displeasing and disagreeable to others.
Knowing this, friends, a bhikkhu should arouse the thought: “I shall be free from envy and free from miserliness.”
‘This person who is crafty and deceitful is displeasing and disagreeable to me;
but if I were also crafty and deceitful, I too would be displeasing and disagreeable to others.
Knowing this, friends, a bhikkhu should arouse the thought: “I shall be without craft and without deceit.”
‘This person who is stubborn and conceited is displeasing and disagreeable to me;
but if I were also stubborn and conceited, I too would be displeasing and disagreeable to others.
Knowing this, friends, a bhikkhu should arouse the thought: ‘I shall be free from stubbornness and free from conceit.’
‘This person who clings to his own views, who is obstinate and hard to relinquish—this person is displeasing and disagreeable to me.
If I were likewise one who clings to my own views, who is obstinate and hard to relinquish, I too would be displeasing and disagreeable to others.
Knowing this, friends, a bhikkhu should arouse the thought: ‘I shall not cling to my own views, I shall not be obstinate, and I shall be easy to relinquish.’”
In this regard, friends, a bhikkhu should examine himself thus:
‘Am I one who has evil desires, one who has fallen under the sway of evil desires?
Friends, if, upon examining himself, a bhikkhu knows thus:
‘I am one of evil desires, fallen under the sway of evil desires,’ then, friends, that bhikkhu should strive for the abandoning of those very same evil, unwholesome states.
But if, friends, while reviewing, a bhikkhu knows thus:
‘I am not one of evil desires, nor have I fallen under the sway of evil desires,’ then, friends, that bhikkhu should dwell in that very joy and gladness, training day and night in wholesome states.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu should examine himself in this way:
"Am I one who lauds myself and disparages others?
If, friends, while examining himself, a bhikkhu knows thus:
‘I am one who praises myself and disparages others,’ then, friends, that bhikkhu should strive for the abandoning of those very same evil, unwholesome states.
But if, friends, while reflecting, a bhikkhu knows:
‘I am not one who praises myself nor disparage others,’ then, friends, that bhikkhu should dwell in that very joy and gladness, training day and night in wholesome states.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu should examine himself in this way:
‘Am I indeed prone to anger, overcome by anger?
Friends, if, upon examining himself, a bhikkhu knows thus:
“Friend, if upon reviewing he knows: ‘I am prone to anger and overcome by anger,’ then that bhikkhu should strive for the abandoning of those very same evil, unwholesome states.
But if, friend, while reviewing, the bhikkhu knows:
‘I am not prone to anger nor overcome by anger,’ then that bhikkhu should dwell in that very joy and gladness, training day and night in wholesome states.”
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu should examine himself in this way:
"Am I indeed prone to anger, and do I harbor resentment because of anger?

Friends, if upon examination a bhikkhu knows: "I am indeed prone to anger, and I harbor resentment because of anger," then that bhikkhu should strive for the abandoning of those very same evil, unwholesome states.

But if, friends, while reflecting, a bhikkhu knows thus: ‘I am not angry, nor do I harbor resentment because of anger,’ then, friends, that bhikkhu should dwell in that very joy and gladness, training day and night in wholesome states.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu should reflect upon himself in this way:
‘Am I indeed prone to anger, and do I become attached because of anger?
If, friends, upon reflection a bhikkhu knows:
‘I am indeed prone to anger, and I become attached because of anger,’ then, friends, that bhikkhu should strive for the abandoning of those very same evil, unwholesome states.
But if, friends, while reflecting, a bhikkhu knows thus:
"I am not angry, nor do I cling because of anger," then, friends, that bhikkhu should dwell in that very joy and gladness, training day and night in wholesome states.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu should reflect upon himself in this way:
‘Am I indeed prone to anger, or do I utter speech that borders on anger?
If, friends, upon reflection a bhikkhu knows:
‘I am indeed prone to anger, and I utter speech that borders on anger,’ then, friends, that bhikkhu should strive for the abandoning of those very same evil, unwholesome states.
But if, friends, while reflecting, a bhikkhu knows thus:
"I am not angry, nor do I utter speech bordering on anger," then, friends, that bhikkhu should dwell in that very joy and gladness, training day and night in wholesome states.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu should reflect upon himself in this way:
‘Am I, when reproved by the reprover, counter-argue with the reprover?

If, friends, upon reflection a bhikkhu knows: ‘When reproved by the reprover, I do counter-argue with the reprover,’ then that bhikkhu, friends, should strive for the abandoning of those very same evil, unwholesome states.
But if, friends, while reflecting, a bhikkhu knows thus:
"I have been reproved by a reprover, yet I did not counter-reprove the reprover," then, friends, that bhikkhu should dwell in that very joy and gladness, training day and night in wholesome states.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu should reflect upon himself in this way:
‘Am I being reproved by this reprover, yet am I dismissing the reprover?

If, friends, upon reflection a bhikkhu knows: ‘I am being reproved by this reprover, yet I am dismissing the reprover,’ then that bhikkhu, friends, should strive for the abandoning of those very same evil, unwholesome states.
But if, friends, upon reflection a bhikkhu knows thus:
‘I have been reproved by the reprover, yet I do not rebuff the reprover’—with that very joy and gladness, friends, that monk should dwell, training day and night in wholesome states.
Furthermore, friends, a monk should reflect within himself thus:
‘When I have been reproved by the reprover, do I indeed counter-accuse the reprover?’”
If, friends, while examining himself, a bhikkhu knows:
"I have been reproved by the reprover, and I am counter-reproving the reprover," then that bhikkhu should strive for the abandoning of those very same evil, unwholesome states.
But if, friends, while examining himself, a bhikkhu knows thus:
‘I have been reproved by the reprover, yet I do not counter-reprove the reprover. With that very joy and gladness, friends, that bhikkhu should dwell, training day and night in wholesome states.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu should examine himself thus:
‘When I am reproved by the reprover, do I evade one thing with another, do I divert the discussion to external matters, and do I manifest anger, hatred, and resentment?’”
If, friends, while reflecting, a bhikkhu knows thus:
"When I am reproved by a reprover, I evade one thing with another, I turn the conversation to external matters, and I manifest anger, hatred,
and resentment," then, friends, that bhikkhu— regarding those very same evil unwholesome states— should [apply himself].
One should strive for the abandoning of those states.
But if, friend, while reflecting, a bhikkhu knows thus:
"I am reproved by the reprover; I do not evade one thing with another, nor do I divert the conversation to external matters..."
‘I am manifesting anger, hatred, and resentment,’ then, friends, that bhikkhu should dwell with that very joy and gladness,
training day and night in wholesome states.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu should examine himself in this way:
‘Why is it that when I am reproved by a reprover, I do not make amends?
If, friends, upon reflection a bhikkhu knows:
‘When I am reproved by a reprover, I do not make amends,’ then, friends, that bhikkhu should strive for the abandoning of those very same evil, unwholesome states.
But if, friends, while reflecting, a bhikkhu knows thus:
‘When I am reproved by a reprover, I manage the matter of the reproach,’ then, friends, that bhikkhu should dwell in that very joy and gladness, training day and night in wholesome states.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu should reflect upon himself in this way:
‘Am I indeed one who is contemptuous and insolent?
If, friends, upon reflection a bhikkhu knows:
‘I am contemptuous and insolent,’ then that bhikkhu should strive for the abandoning of those very same evil, unwholesome states.
But if, friends, while examining himself, a bhikkhu knows thus:
‘I am free from malice and free from ill will,’ then, friends, that bhikkhu should dwell in that very joy and gladness, training day and night in wholesome states.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu should examine himself in this way:
‘Am I indeed envious and miserly?
If, friends, upon reflection a monk knows:
‘I am envious and miserly,’ then that monk, friends, should strive for the abandoning of those very same evil, unwholesome states.
But if, friends, while reflecting, a bhikkhu knows thus:
‘I am free from envy and free from stinginess,’ then, friends, that bhikkhu should dwell in that very joy and gladness, training day and night in wholesome states.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu should reflect upon himself in this way:
‘Am I indeed a deceiver and a hypocrite?
If, friends, upon reflection a monk knows thus:
‘I am a deceiver and a hypocrite,’ then, friends, that monk should strive for the abandoning of those very same evil, unwholesome states.
But if, friends, while reviewing himself, a bhikkhu knows thus:
"I am not crafty; I am not deceitful," then, friends, that bhikkhu should dwell in that very joy and gladness, training day and night in wholesome states.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu should review himself in this way:
‘Am I indeed stubborn and conceited?
If, friends, upon reflection a bhikkhu knows:
‘I am stubborn and conceited,’ then that bhikkhu should strive for the abandoning of those very same evil, unwholesome states.
But if, friends, while reflecting, a bhikkhu knows thus:
‘I am not haughty and I am not conceited,’ then, friends, that bhikkhu should dwell in that very joy and gladness, training day and night in wholesome states.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu should reflect upon himself in this way:
‘Am I one who clings to my own views, who is obstinate and hard to relinquish?
If, friends, upon reflection a bhikkhu knows:
‘I am one who clings to my own views, who is obstinate and hard to relinquish,’ then that bhikkhu, friends, should strive for the abandoning of those very same evil, unwholesome states.
But if, friends, while examining himself, a bhikkhu knows thus:

"I am not one who misapprehends through mere views, I am not one who obstinately clings, and I am one who relinquishes well," then, friends, that bhikkhu should dwell in that very joy and gladness, training day and night in wholesome states.
If, friends, while examining himself, a bhikkhu sees that all these evil, unwholesome states have not yet been abandoned within him...

If, friend, a bhikkhu, upon reviewing himself, perceives that all these evil, unwholesome states have been abandoned within him, then, friend, that bhikkhu should strive for the abandonment of all these very same evil, unwholesome states.
If he perceives [any fault], then, friends, that bhikkhu should dwell in that very joy and gladness, training day and night in wholesome states.
Just as, friends, a woman or a man— young, youthful, fond of ornaments—
looking at the reflection of their own face in a clean, polished mirror or in a clear bowl of water, if there...
If he sees dust or a stain, he strives for the abandoning of that very dust or stain;
but if he does not see dust or a stain there, he is satisfied by that:
"It is a gain for me, indeed! My [mind] is truly pure!"
In the same way, friends, if a bhikkhu, upon reviewing himself, perceives that all these evil, unwholesome states have not been abandoned within him, then, friends,
that bhikkhu should strive for the abandonment of all these evil, unwholesome states.
"But if, friends, while reflecting, a bhikkhu perceives within himself that all these evil, unwholesome states have been abandoned, then, friends,
that bhikkhu should dwell in that very joy and gladness, training day and night in wholesome states."
Thus spoke the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna.
The bhikkhus were uplifted and rejoiced in the words of the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna.
The fifth discourse, the *Anumānasutta*, is concluded.
